prompt:
# Write one behaviour-tree node that ADJUSTS an existing navigator

You are writing a single node for the behaviour tree of a Unitree Go2 quadruped
navigating an indoor space it has no map of.

Below the node is an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy. The
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`. You never
touch the policy, the gait, or the joints.

**You are not writing the navigator.** A navigator already exists, it already
drives, and it will keep driving whether or not your node does anything. Your
node sits above it and revises what it asked for.

Return **one Python module**, in one fenced ```python block, and nothing else
that looks like code. Everything you want to say in prose, say outside the
fence. What the module must contain is set out in "What to return" at the end.

## How the tree runs: a layered command pipeline

Every node in the tree ticks, **every step, in order**. Nothing short-circuits
anything.

    Layer[ ports, BASE, node_1, node_2, ... ]
             ^      ^      ^
             |      |      `- each may revise the fields it declared
             |      `-------- proposes a whole command, every tick
             `--------------- publishes a few facts from the sensors

The **base** is a general indoor navigator. It gets the robot most of the way
most of the time, it handles the awkward cases, and it never declines to act.
Each later node may then adjust individual fields of what the base proposed.

This is subsumption: a competent low layer, refined by narrow higher ones. Your
node is one of the higher ones.

**So the thing you are writing is small.** It does one thing to one part of the
command, under one condition, and the rest of the time it stays out of the way.

## The one hard rule: you declare which fields you may write

Your class declares `WRITES` — the Twist fields it is allowed to touch:

```python
WRITES = ("vx",)            # may bound or set forward speed, nothing else
WRITES = ("wz",)            # may steer, but may not change speed
WRITES = ("vx", "wz")       # both. Only if the mechanism genuinely needs both.
```

This is **enforced, not advisory.** Writing a field you did not declare raises
immediately and the node is rejected. Declare the smallest set your mechanism
actually needs — a node that declares all three is claiming to be a navigator,
and it will be judged as one.

Two ways to write, and they are the only two:

```python
ports.cap(vx=0.35)       # min(|pending|, 0.35), sign kept. Never speeds up.
ports.adjust(wz=0.8)     # replaces the field outright. Last writer wins.
```

Prefer `cap` whenever the mechanism is a limit, a bound, or a "no faster than"
— it composes with other caps in any order, which `adjust` does not.

And you can see what the base asked for:

```python
pending = ports.command          # a Command(vx, vy, wz). Never None when you
                                 # tick, because the base ticks before you.
if pending.vx > my_limit:
    ports.cap(vx=my_limit)
```

**Do not call `ports.drive(...)`.** That writes the whole command and is the
base's job; it raises for a node that narrowed `WRITES`.

## Declining is a first-class outcome, and it is free

Return `Status.FAILURE` from `precondition`, or simply write nothing in `tick`,
and the base's command passes through **byte-identical**. The robot behaves
exactly as if your node were not in the tree.

That matters more than it sounds. Your node's contribution is measured by adding
it to the tree and re-running the same worlds: it can only be credited for the
episodes it changes, and it is blamed for every episode it breaks. A node that
acts only when its trigger genuinely holds is a good node. A node that fires on
every tick has replaced the base rather than supported it, and it will be
measured as having done so.

## The node contract

A leaf is one of three kinds, and the kind is the class you subclass:

- **`Condition`** — answers one question about the world and publishes it as a
  port. Never touches the Twist.
- **`Action`** — the only kind that may touch the Twist. With a narrowed
  `WRITES` it is a *modifier*, which is what you are writing.
- **`Decorator`** — wraps exactly one child and governs whether the child runs.
  Never touches the Twist itself.

Your class declares, as class attributes:

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `WRITES` | the Twist fields this node may write. See above. |
| `PORTS` | a tuple of `Port` — the typed interface between nodes. See below. |
| `PRECONDITION` | one sentence: when this node applies |
| `EFFECT` | one sentence: what this node changes |
| `TAGS` | a tuple of short strings, for retrieval |

and implements:

```python
def reset(self, scenario, rng):    # clear per-episode state. optional.
def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:   # default: always True
def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:         # Status.SUCCESS / FAILURE / RUNNING
```

**One precondition and one effect.** A node that needs two of either is two
nodes. This is not a style rule: contribution is measured by adding one node at
a time, and a node with two effects is attributable to neither.

**No coupling to a specific scenario.** Your node will be run on procedurally
generated worlds you have never seen. It may not name a room, a coordinate, a
doorway or a map. Anything it knows about the world it learns through `obs` at
tick time.

### Ports

Ports are how nodes pass information to each other. They are **not** a
blackboard: at tick time you are handed a `PortView` restricted to exactly the
ports you declared, and touching anything else raises immediately.

```python
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.IN)    # you read it:   value = ports["name"]
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.OUT)   # you write it:  ports["name"] = value
```

The port vocabulary is **closed**. These seven types and no others:

| `PortType` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `POSE` | `(x, y, yaw)` — a belief about where the robot is, never ground truth |
| `BEARING` | radians, robot frame unless the port name says otherwise |
| `SPEED` | m/s, non-negative |
| `RANGES` | an array of beam returns, metres |
| `CONFIDENCE` | `[0, 1]` — how much to trust something |
| `FLAG` | a boolean fact about the episode |
| `REGION` | an area of the floor, `(x, y, radius)` |

Three ports are always published before your node ticks, so you may declare any
of them as inputs: `goal_known` (FLAG), `pose` (POSE), `ranges` (RANGES).
Anything else you declare as an input must be published by another node earlier
in the Layer, and if nothing does, the tree refuses to build.

Publish an OUT port when the quantity you computed is genuinely useful to
someone else — a limit, a bearing, a confidence. Do not publish your own
internal state.

### What to import

Exactly these, and nothing else.

```python
import math
import numpy as np

from core.observation import Command
from nodes.contract import (Action, Condition, Decorator, Direction, Port,
                            PortType, Status)
```

Import only what you use. You will usually not need `Command` at all: a modifier
revises fields, it does not construct commands.

### What your node can see

`tick` is handed an `Observation`, frozen, one per control step:

```python
obs.t                   # sim seconds since the episode started
obs.ranges              # np.ndarray, 181 beams, metres, inf where no return
obs.range_angles        # np.ndarray, beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
obs.range_max           # 6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
obs.pose_estimate       # (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, not the truth
obs.pose_error_estimate # scalar, metres — how wrong we think the belief is
obs.contact             # bool — are we touching something right now
obs.goal                # (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of these are traps and both are deliberate:

- **`pose_estimate` is a belief.** On some scenarios a seeded random walk is
  added to it and it drifts away from the truth. Ground truth is never in
  `Observation`; the runner keeps it for scoring only.
- **`obs.goal` may be `None`**, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still
  scored against it, but this robot has not found it yet. It **latches**: once
  disclosed it stays disclosed. Your node runs on scenarios that withhold the
  goal and on scenarios that do not, so **handle `None` explicitly**. Do not
  assume a tuple.

The scan is 181 beams over a full circle, so `obs.ranges[0]` is not the front —
find the beam you want through `obs.range_angles`.

Speeds are saturated by the runner to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and
`|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Asking for more is not an error; it is just clipped.

## The task family this node has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is known, in an indoor space with no map. Walls and furniture occlude; the route is not a straight line and the obstruction is often not visible until the robot is close to it.

## What to base the node on

A principle card has been written for this task. **Implement this principle and
nothing else.**

```yaml
id: geometric_boundary_reorientation
node_name: ReorientToBoundaryGeometry

mechanism: Cheng found that a disoriented rat re-establishes its spatial frame from the metric shape of the extended surface layout — the relative lengths and arrangement of the bounding walls — and not from featural cues attached to places, even when those features are salient and would fully disambiguate the location. The signature of this is the rotational error: in a rectangular arena the animal searched at the correct corner and at the corner related to it by a 180-degree rotation at approximately equal rates, because those two corners are indistinguishable to a purely geometric representation. Two things follow that matter for a robot. First, the boundary shape is a heading reference that does not accumulate error: unlike dead reckoning, the walls do not drift, so re-anchoring belief to them cancels accumulated odometric error rather than compounding it. Second, that reference is only ever determined up to the symmetry group of the shape, so a reorientation system built on it must refuse any correction large enough to be a symmetry-induced misassignment instead of committing to it. The mechanism is therefore: when the pose belief is suspect, freeze translation, extract the principal axis of the surrounding surface layout, and rotate the believed yaw onto the axis frame that was recorded while the belief was still trustworthy — accepting only corrections small enough to be unambiguous under that symmetry.

trigger: Fires when the robot's own confidence in its pose belief has degraded past a threshold while a usable boundary is visible: pose_error_estimate exceeds 0.5 m, AND the current scan defines an axis (see derivation: enough finite returns, sufficiently elongated return cloud), AND at least 5.0 s of sim time has elapsed since this node last completed. It does not fire when the belief is trusted, when the visible surroundings are too open or too rotationally symmetric to define an axis, or when the required correction turns out to exceed the unambiguous range.

derivation: All numbers here are mine; Cheng's arena and metric do not transfer directly. (1) Axis extraction. Take the beams with finite range below range_max = 6.0 m, convert to robot-frame points p_i = r_i * (cos a_i, sin a_i), subtract their centroid, and form the 2x2 second-moment matrix. Its eigenvectors give the principal axis of the visible surface layout; the axis is an undirected line, so it is defined modulo 180 degrees. This is the sensor analogue of "shape of the extended surfaces": it is dominated by walls, which subtend many beams, and is insensitive to any single feature, which subtends few — the encapsulation from features is preserved by construction. (2) Admissibility. Require at least 40 of the 181 beams finite (about 22% of the circle; below that the cloud is a fragment and the moment matrix is dominated by one wall segment), and require eigenvalue ratio lambda_min/lambda_max < 0.6, i.e. the cloud is at least modestly elongated. A ratio near 1.0 means a rotationally symmetric view — an open floor or a square room centre — where Cheng's module has nothing to lock onto and the correction would be arbitrary. If either test fails, the node returns FAILURE and changes nothing. (3) Reference frame. Whenever pose_error_estimate <= 0.25 m (half the trigger threshold, so the reference is only ever laid down while the belief is clearly trusted), store the axis in world coordinates: theta_ref = yaw_belief + axis_angle_robot, wrapped into [0, 90) degrees, i.e. reduced modulo the 90-degree rectilinear symmetry of an indoor layout, together with an exponential average over the last 2.0 s to smooth gait-induced body sway. (4) Correction. On fire, command vx = vy = wz = 0 for 0.5 s while averaging the axis over the scans in that window — the frozen locomotion policy sways the body, and standing still is cheaper than modelling the sway. Then compute d = wrap_to_pm45(theta_ref - (yaw_belief + axis_angle_robot)), where wrap_to_pm45 reduces modulo 90 degrees into [-45, +45). Apply yaw_belief += d, leave x and y untouched, and reduce pose_error_estimate by the component of it that heading error explains — conservatively, multiply it by 0.7 rather than zeroing it, since the position belief is not corrected. (5) The refusal, which is the part that comes straight from the rotational error. |d| is capped at 45 degrees by construction, and if the pre-wrap residual lands within 5 degrees of the +/-45-degree boundary the assignment between adjacent symmetry copies is a coin flip; in that case apply nothing and return FAILURE. Cheng's rats committed the rotational error; a robot that commits it injects a 90- or 180-degree heading error into a belief that was merely noisy, which is strictly worse than doing nothing. (6) Scale justification for the 0.5 m trigger: the Go2 is about 0.70 m long and 0.31 m wide, and indoor free passages are commonly 0.8-0.9 m; a positional or heading-induced belief error above roughly 0.5 m is enough to aim the robot at a door jamb instead of the opening, so that is where re-anchoring starts to pay for the time it costs.

prediction:
  statement: On scenarios where pose_estimate drifts, a controller that periodically re-anchors its believed yaw to the principal axis of the visible surface layout reaches the goal on a higher fraction of seeds than a goal_seeker that integrates its drifting belief unchecked, because heading error is the component of belief error that grows without bound into cross-track error over a long route, and the boundary is a non-drifting reference for it.
  metric: goal_reached
  baseline: goal_seeker
  min_effect: 0.15
  cost_metric: time_to_goal
```

The fields mean what they say, and each one has a job:

- **mechanism** — what happens, and why it helps. This is the node body.
- **trigger** — when it applies. This is the precondition, and under the layered
  pipeline it is doing real work: outside the trigger your node must leave the
  base's command alone.
- **derivation** — how the principle becomes a rule for a Go2 with a 181-beam 2D
  scan. Where the derivation and your instincts disagree, follow the derivation:
  it is what the card is for.
- **prediction** — the falsifiable claim. **Restate it verbatim** in
  `PREDICTION`: the metric, the baseline and the minimum effect are the card's,
  not yours.
- **node_name** — what the leaf is called. Use it as the class name.

You are not told where this principle came from, and you do not need to know.
A card is a card: extracted from a paper, recalled from one, or devised from
nothing, it is implemented the same way and judged by the same harness.

If you believe a different mechanism would score better, that belief is not what
is being measured here — a node that quietly implements something else makes the
card untestable.

**If the principle genuinely cannot be expressed as an adjustment to an existing
navigator, say so in prose and write the closest honest version you can.** Some
mechanisms are whole navigators and this pipeline cannot represent them; that is
a finding about the corpus, and it is more useful than a node that pretends.

## How this node will be judged

Two steps, both automatic, neither of which you can talk round.

1. **Validity.** Your module is loaded, wired into
   `Layer[ports, BASE, your node]`, and ticked over a rollout. It has to build,
   its ports have to be satisfiable, and it must not raise. Writing a Twist
   field you did not declare fails here.
2. **Contribution.** The tree above is run over a suite of randomly generated
   indoor worlds and compared, on identical worlds, against the base alone. What
   is reported is how many worlds your node **fixed** (the base failed, the pair
   succeeded) and how many it **broke** (the reverse).

You do not write the worlds and you have never seen them. There is no
micro-world to build and no baseline to name — that is deliberate, because a
generator that writes both the mechanism and the world that judges it is
grading its own homework.

## Rules the candidate is checked against

Your module is rejected, automatically, if any of these is false. The rejection
is recorded with its reason; it is not a catastrophe, but it is a wasted node.

- It parses, and it imports **only** from this list:
  `math`, `numpy`, `core.observation`, `nodes.contract`, `harness.micro`.
  Nothing else — no `os`, no file access, no `core.scenario`, no `core.geometry`.
  Your node learns about the world through `obs`, and that restriction is what
  makes "no coupling to a specific scenario" true rather than promised.
- It defines **exactly one** `Condition`, `Action` or `Decorator` subclass.
- Every port type is one of the seven. `EFFECT` and `PRECONDITION` are non-empty.
- `WRITES` names only `vx`, `vy` and `wz`, and the node writes nothing outside
  it.

## What to return

One fenced ```python block. It contains exactly two things:

1. **One node class** — normally an `Action` with a narrowed `WRITES`.
2. **`PREDICTION`** — a module-level dict, the card's falsifiable claim:

   ```python
   PREDICTION = {
       "metric": "goal_reached",     # what gets better
       "baseline": "base",           # what it gets better than
       "min_effect": 0.5,            # by at least how much
       "cost_metric": "time_to_goal" # what it makes WORSE. Required, and honest.
   }
   ```

   `cost_metric` may be `""` only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs
   nothing, and you should be suspicious of that belief.

**No `micro()`.** Do not write one; it is not read.

Put a short docstring on the class saying what mechanism it implements, which
Twist field it revises and why, and when it declines. Write it as you would
write code someone else has to maintain: comments where a choice is not obvious,
and no comments restating the line below them.

response.text:
The card's actual effect — `yaw_belief += d`, `pose_error_estimate *= 0.7` — **is not expressible in this pipeline.** `Observation` is frozen and handed to me; the only things a node emits are Twist fields and ports. There is no belief-writing channel, and no node downstream of me can write one either. So a literal implementation is impossible, and I want to be explicit about that rather than quietly pretend.

The closest honest version follows from asking what a belief edit *does* to the Twist. If the base steers on the robot-frame goal bearing `b = β − yaw_belief` with some gain `k`, then setting `yaw_belief += d` changes its command to `k·(b − d)` on that tick and on every tick after, until the next correction. The exact Twist-space image of the card's step (4) is therefore **a persistent yaw-rate bias of `−k·d`**, not a transient turn. This matters: an in-place rotation of `d` would be worthless here, because turning the body changes belief and truth by the same amount, leaves the error untouched, and the base simply unwinds it within a second. Only a sustained bias reproduces the belief edit. `k` is unknown, so I use a fixed gain with a hard clip; the sign is exactly right and the base's own feedback bounds the resulting heading offset, which is the conservative failure mode.

Everything upstream of the effect is implemented as derived, unmodified: second-moment axis extraction over finite sub-`range_max` returns, the ≥40-beam and λmin/λmax < 0.6 admissibility tests, the reference latched only while `pose_error_estimate ≤ 0.25` with a 2.0 s exponential average, reduction modulo the 90° rectilinear symmetry, the 0.5 s freeze with the axis averaged over that window, and the refusal — if the residual lands within 5° of the ±45° boundary the node applies nothing and returns FAILURE, because committing Cheng's rotational error injects a 90° heading error into a belief that was merely noisy.

Two deliberate choices beyond the card. `WRITES = ("vx", "wz")`: the mechanism needs both because the derivation's measurement step *is* a translation freeze, and the correction *is* a heading change; I leave `vy` alone rather than claim all three. And the bias is suppressed while something is within 1.0 m ahead or on contact — a do-no-harm guard, not a second effect, because a standing yaw bias applied during the base's local avoidance is the one way this node could plausibly drive the robot into a wall. The bias decays with a 6 s time constant, slightly longer than the 5 s re-trigger interval, so it persists between corrections but fades out rather than steering the robot forever on a stale measurement.

On scenarios without drift the trigger never holds, no reference is ever consumed, and the base's command passes through byte-identical.

```python
import math

import numpy as np

from nodes.contract import Action, Direction, Port, PortType, Status


class ReorientToBoundaryGeometry(Action):
    """Re-anchors heading to the metric shape of the surrounding surface layout.

    Implements geometric boundary reorientation: when the robot's own pose-error
    estimate says the belief has gone bad, the principal axis of the visible
    range cloud is compared against the axis recorded while the belief was still
    trusted, and the difference -- reduced modulo the 90-degree symmetry of a
    rectilinear indoor layout -- is the accumulated heading error. Walls subtend
    many beams and furniture subtends few, so the second-moment axis is a
    wall-dominated, non-drifting heading reference.

    The card's effect is a write to the pose belief, which this pipeline cannot
    express. Its exact image on the Twist is used instead: a belief edit of +d
    shifts the base's robot-frame goal bearing by -d on every subsequent tick, so
    the correction is applied as a sustained bias on ``wz`` rather than a
    one-shot turn (turning the body moves belief and truth together and corrects
    nothing). ``vx`` is capped to zero for the 0.5 s measurement window because
    the derivation asks for a translation freeze while the axis is averaged --
    standing still is cheaper than modelling gait-induced body sway.

    Declines, leaving the base's command untouched, when: the belief is trusted,
    no reference axis has been laid down yet, the view is too open (<40 finite
    returns) or too rotationally symmetric (eigenvalue ratio >= 0.6) to define an
    axis, fewer than 5 s have passed since the last attempt, the residual lands
    within 5 degrees of the +/-45-degree symmetry boundary where the assignment
    between adjacent symmetry copies is a coin flip, or an obstacle is close
    enough ahead that the base is plainly doing local avoidance.
    """

    WRITES = ("vx", "wz")
    PORTS = (Port("boundary_yaw_correction", PortType.BEARING, Direction.OUT),)
    PRECONDITION = (
        "The pose-error estimate exceeds 0.5 m while a boundary axis is usable, "
        "or a boundary-referenced heading correction is currently being applied, "
        "or the belief is trusted enough to refresh the reference axis."
    )
    EFFECT = (
        "Re-anchors heading to the remembered wall-axis frame by freezing "
        "translation for 0.5 s to measure the axis and then biasing the base's "
        "yaw rate by the accepted correction."
    )
    TAGS = ("reorientation", "boundary", "geometry", "drift", "heading", "yaw")

    # Trigger / trust thresholds (metres of believed pose error).
    _ERR_TRIGGER = 0.5
    _ERR_TRUST = 0.25

    # Axis admissibility.
    _MIN_FINITE = 40
    _MAX_EIG_RATIO = 0.6

    # Timing (seconds).
    _REF_TAU = 2.0
    _FREEZE = 0.5
    _COOLDOWN = 5.0
    _BIAS_TAU = 6.0

    # Symmetry refusal: |d| is capped at 45 deg by construction; within 5 deg of
    # that boundary the symmetry-copy assignment is a coin flip.
    _QUARTER = math.pi / 2.0
    _REFUSE_MARGIN = math.radians(5.0)

    # Correction bias. The base's steering gain is unknown, so the gain is fixed
    # and hard-clipped; the base's own feedback bounds the resulting offset.
    _BIAS_GAIN = 1.0
    _BIAS_MAX = 0.35

    # Do-no-harm guard on the bias.
    _GUARD_RANGE = 1.0
    _GUARD_HALF_ANGLE = math.radians(60.0)

    def reset(self, scenario, rng):
        self._t_prev = None
        self._ref_vec = None
        self._meas_vec = None
        self._meas_n = 0
        self._meas_t0 = None
        self._last_attempt_t = None
        self._bias_d = 0.0
        self._bias_t = None
        self._published = 0.0

    def _state(self):
        if not hasattr(self, "_t_prev"):
            self.reset(None, None)

    def precondition(self, obs, ports):
        self._state()
        err = float(obs.pose_error_estimate)
        if self._meas_t0 is not None:
            return True
        if err > self._ERR_TRIGGER:
            return True
        if self._bias_t is not None and abs(self._bias_d) > 1e-3:
            return True
        # Ticking on a trusted belief does not write anything; it is how the
        # reference axis gets laid down in the first place.
        return err <= self._ERR_TRUST

    def tick(self, obs, ports):
        self._state()
        t = float(obs.t)
        dt = 0.0 if self._t_prev is None else max(0.0, min(1.0, t - self._t_prev))
        self._t_prev = t

        axis = self._axis_angle(obs)
        err = float(obs.pose_error_estimate)
        yaw = float(obs.pose_estimate[2])
        theta = None if axis is None else (yaw + axis) % self._QUARTER

        # (3) Reference frame: recorded only while the belief is clearly trusted.
        if theta is not None and err <= self._ERR_TRUST and self._meas_t0 is None:
            self._update_reference(theta, dt)

        if self._meas_t0 is not None:
            return self._measure(obs, ports, t, theta)

        if (err > self._ERR_TRIGGER
                and self._ref_vec is not None
                and theta is not None
                and (self._last_attempt_t is None
                     or t - self._last_attempt_t >= self._COOLDOWN)):
            self._meas_t0 = t
            self._meas_vec = np.zeros(2)
            self._meas_n = 0
            return self._measure(obs, ports, t, theta)

        return self._apply_bias(obs, ports, t)

    # -- axis extraction ---------------------------------------------------

    def _axis_angle(self, obs):
        """Principal axis of the visible surface layout, robot frame, mod pi."""
        r = np.asarray(obs.ranges, dtype=float)
        a = np.asarray(obs.range_angles, dtype=float)
        if r.size == 0 or a.size != r.size:
            return None
        keep = np.isfinite(r) & (r > 0.0) & (r < float(obs.range_max))
        n = int(np.count_nonzero(keep))
        if n < self._MIN_FINITE:
            return None

        rr = r[keep]
        aa = a[keep]
        pts = np.stack((rr * np.cos(aa), rr * np.sin(aa)), axis=1)
        pts = pts - pts.mean(axis=0)
        cov = (pts.T @ pts) / float(n)
        if not np.all(np.isfinite(cov)):
            return None
        try:
            evals, evecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)
        except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
            return None

        lam_min = float(evals[0])
        lam_max = float(evals[1])
        if lam_max <= 1e-9:
            return None
        # Ratio near 1.0 is an open floor or a room centre: nothing to lock onto.
        if lam_min / lam_max >= self._MAX_EIG_RATIO:
            return None

        v = evecs[:, 1]
        return math.atan2(float(v[1]), float(v[0])) % math.pi

    def _update_reference(self, theta, dt):
        v = self._unit4(theta)
        if self._ref_vec is None:
            self._ref_vec = v
            return
        alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-dt / self._REF_TAU) if dt > 0.0 else 0.0
        self._ref_vec = (1.0 - alpha) * self._ref_vec + alpha * v

    @staticmethod
    def _unit4(theta):
        # Angles live modulo 90 deg, so quadruple before averaging on the circle.
        return np.array([math.cos(4.0 * theta), math.sin(4.0 * theta)])

    @staticmethod
    def _from4(vec):
        return (math.atan2(float(vec[1]), float(vec[0])) / 4.0) % (math.pi / 2.0)

    def _wrap_pm45(self, angle):
        return (angle + math.pi / 4.0) % self._QUARTER - math.pi / 4.0

    # -- states ------------------------------------------------------------

    def _measure(self, obs, ports, t, theta):
        """(4) Freeze, averaging the axis over the scans in the window."""
        ports.cap(vx=0.0)
        ports.cap(wz=0.0)
        ports["boundary_yaw_correction"] = 0.0
        self._published = 0.0

        if theta is not None:
            self._meas_vec = self._meas_vec + self._unit4(theta)
            self._meas_n += 1

        if t - self._meas_t0 < self._FREEZE:
            return Status.RUNNING

        self._meas_t0 = None
        self._last_attempt_t = t
        n, vec = self._meas_n, self._meas_vec
        self._meas_n, self._meas_vec = 0, None

        if n < 3 or float(np.hypot(vec[0], vec[1])) < 1e-6:
            return Status.FAILURE

        d = self._wrap_pm45(self._from4(self._ref_vec) - self._from4(vec))

        # (5) The refusal. Committing a symmetry-induced misassignment would put
        # a 90-degree error into a belief that was merely noisy.
        if abs(d) > math.pi / 4.0 - self._REFUSE_MARGIN:
            return Status.FAILURE

        self._bias_d = d
        self._bias_t = t
        return Status.SUCCESS

    def _apply_bias(self, obs, ports, t):
        """Twist-space image of ``yaw_belief += d``: a sustained yaw-rate bias."""
        if self._bias_t is None or abs(self._bias_d) <= 1e-3:
            ports["boundary_yaw_correction"] = 0.0
            self._published = 0.0
            return Status.FAILURE

        age = t - self._bias_t
        if age > 3.0 * self._BIAS_TAU:
            self._bias_d = 0.0
            self._bias_t = None
            ports["boundary_yaw_correction"] = 0.0
            self._published = 0.0
            return Status.FAILURE

        decay = math.exp(-age / self._BIAS_TAU)
        correction = self._bias_d * decay
        ports["boundary_yaw_correction"] = float(correction)
        self._published = float(correction)

        if self._blocked_ahead(obs):
            return Status.FAILURE

        bias = -self._BIAS_GAIN * correction
        bias = max(-self._BIAS_MAX, min(self._BIAS_MAX, bias))
        ports.adjust(wz=float(ports.command.wz + bias))
        return Status.SUCCESS

    def _blocked_ahead(self, obs):
        if bool(obs.contact):
            return True
        r = np.asarray(obs.ranges, dtype=float)
        a = np.asarray(obs.range_angles, dtype=float)
        if r.size == 0 or a.size != r.size:
            return False
        signed = np.arctan2(np.sin(a), np.cos(a))
        front = np.isfinite(r) & (np.abs(signed) <= self._GUARD_HALF_ANGLE)
        if not np.any(front):
            return False
        return float(np.min(r[front])) < self._GUARD_RANGE


PREDICTION = {
    "metric": "goal_reached",
    "baseline": "goal_seeker",
    "min_effect": 0.15,
    "cost_metric": "time_to_goal",
}
```

The cost is honest and structural: up to 0.5 s of standstill per 5 s whenever the belief is bad and the view is usable, plus whatever path lengthening the bias causes when the drift estimate is imperfect — `time_to_goal` gets worse on exactly the seeds where `goal_reached` is supposed to get better.
